title: useEffect — and when not to use it
objectives: Explain that effects exist to sync with systems outside React, like a socket, timer, or the network
Write a subscription effect whose cleanup and deps reconnect cleanly when a prop like roomId changes
Predict when an effect runs relative to render, and the stale value an empty-deps interval reads
Fix a fetch effect's race and cancel stale requests by aborting the previous request with AbortController in cleanup, telling that AbortError apart from a real failure

sources.title: React docs: You Might Not Need an Effect

questions.prompt: Which of these genuinely needs a useEffect?

options.text: Computing a user's full name from first + last name
Filtering a list based on a search box value
Subscribing to a WebSocket and updating when messages arrive

questions.explanation: Effects synchronize with systems OUTSIDE React — subscriptions, timers, the DOM, the network. Full name, filtering, and date formatting are all derived during render; doing them in an Effect adds a render and can desync. Only the WebSocket reaches an external system.

questions.prompt: What does the dependency array [roomId] actually promise React?

options.text: Re-run this effect (after cleaning up the previous one) whenever roomId changes
Run the effect only one time, ever
Memoize roomId so it never changes
Debounce the effect until roomId stops changing

questions.explanation: The dependency array is a claim about WHEN to re-synchronize: clean up with the previous values, then re-run with the new ones, whenever a listed value changes (compared with `Object.is`). `[]` means 'never re-run after mount'; omitting the array entirely means 'run after every render'. And `[]` doesn't promise 'exactly once': since React 18, StrictMode in development adds one extra setup + cleanup cycle on mount, which is harmless when the cleanup undoes the setup.

questions.prompt: A search effect fetches results for `query` and calls `setResults` when the response arrives. What must its cleanup do?

options.text: Abort the request, or flag its response to be ignored, so an older query's late response can't overwrite a newer one
Nothing — React drops state updates that come from an effect it has already cleaned up
Set a ref so the effect only fetches the first time, which also stops StrictMode's double fetch
Await the previous request before starting the next, so responses arrive in order

questions.explanation: Responses can arrive in any order, and React doesn't know which `setResults` call is stale — it applies them all. The cleanup runs before the next query's effect, so it's where you mark the old request as dead: `controller.abort()` cancels it (and makes it reject with an `AbortError` you ignore), or an `ignore = true` flag makes its `.then` skip the update. Aborting also stops the wasted network work. A run-once ref breaks the effect for every later query and only hides StrictMode's check; serializing requests makes every search wait for the one before it.

prompts.prompt: Complete the subscription effect: subscribe on mount, re-subscribe when roomId changes, and clean up to avoid leaks.
prompts.explanation: The cleanup tears down the old connection before the next run (and on unmount). Listing roomId re-runs the effect — disconnect old, connect new — on every room change. Omit the cleanup and you leak one connection per switch.

prompts.prompt: Complete the search effect so a query change or an unmount cancels the request still in flight.
prompts.explanation: Each run makes its own `AbortController` and hands its `signal` to `fetch` (the option is named `signal`). React runs the cleanup before the next run and on unmount, so `controller.abort()` cancels exactly the request that run started. The cancelled fetch rejects with an `AbortError` — so it never reaches `.then(setResults)`, which is what fixes the race — and the `.catch` skips that one because it's your own cleanup, not a failure.

snippets.question: What value does the counter show after ~5 seconds, and why?
snippets.explanation: Empty deps → the effect runs once and closes over count = 0 forever (a stale closure). Every tick computes 0 + 1 = 1. Fix with the functional updater setCount(c => c + 1), which receives the latest value and needs no count in the deps. (StrictMode doesn't change the answer: its extra mount cycle runs the cleanup, which clears the first interval before the second starts.)

snippets.question: What is logged on the first render, then after one click?
snippets.explanation: React calls the component (logs 'render n'), commits the result to the DOM, and only then runs effects (logs 'effect n') — with no dependency array, after every render. What's guaranteed is *after commit*, not *after paint*: an effect caused by an interaction like this click may run before the browser paints (react.dev, useEffect caveats); one that isn't usually runs after. In development under StrictMode you'd see more lines — `render 0` twice (React calls the component twice to catch impure rendering), `effect 0` twice (the extra setup + cleanup cycle on mount), then `render 1` twice and `effect 1` once — but the order rule holds.
